If you're weighing up whether to bring machining in-house, part of that question is for a coach and part of it needs a spreadsheet. Coach, consultant and mentor are often talked about as one thing, and a lot of disappointment with advisers starts with asking one of them a question another is better placed to answer.
A coach helps you decide what you want and holds you to it. A consultant brings expertise and tells you what to fix. A mentor tells you what they did when they faced something similar.

Plenty of engineering owners say, fairly, that they don't need anyone to tell them how to run their business. They're right about the decisions only they can make: what they want the business to do for them, and how much risk they'll carry to get it. Coaching fits there. It fits less well where the problem is technical and someone has seen it many times before, such as a costing model that hides loss-making jobs, or an estimating process that depends on one person. Being coached slowly towards an answer a specialist could give you in an afternoon is an expensive way to get it.

Back to that hypothetical in-house decision. Whether the owner wants the extra headcount and capital at this stage of his plans is a coaching question. Whether his volumes and margins justify a machine is a consultant's question, and it needs numbers. A mentor who has made the same move can tell him what caught them out, which is useful as long as he remembers it was their firm and their timing.

Each has a way of going wrong. Mentors drift into autobiography, so the advice becomes "do what I did". Coaches can hold back an answer they already know, for the sake of the method, while the owner pays for the delay. If an adviser offers you all three, ask them to say which one they're doing before they give you their view: "That's your call", "Here's what I've seen go wrong" and "Here's what the numbers say" are different kinds of help.
On a small decision you can reverse, the distinction hardly matters. It matters when the answer costs six figures or can't easily be undone.

A check you can run: think back over your last few conversations with a coach, mentor or adviser. Were you asking for help to decide, for an expert answer, or for someone's experience? And which did you get?
